topics.title: The vocal tract, constrictions and the vowels /i/, /a/ and /u/

blocks.main: **The air in the vocal tract vibrates back and forth along the tube, and it is a fixed-free system.** This means it has one end where the air cannot move and one end where it can. The air is **fixed at the glottis** (the opening between the vocal folds). The closed vocal folds stop the air there from moving, so the air there can only be compressed. The air is **free at the lips**, where it moves in and out.
sub: When the air on both sides of a spot moves toward that spot, the air at that spot gets compressed (packed together). When the air on both sides moves away from the spot, the air there spreads out.
This means the spot where the air moves the least is the spot where it gets compressed the most. The spot where the air moves the most is the spot where it gets compressed the least.
When there is no constriction, as in **done**, the vowel is **schwa** (the neutral vowel sound). Its formants (frequency regions with strong acoustic energy) are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**.
blocks.end: So a constriction does different things depending on where it is placed, because the air moves differently at different places in the tube.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p16 · Lecture 13 · p12 · Lecture 14 · p8
blocks.main: **In the vocal tract, vowels differ in the shape of the tube.** The shape depends on where the tongue makes a constriction and whether the lips are rounded. A **constriction** is a place where the tube becomes narrower. When the tongue is high and toward the front of the mouth, the result is the vowel in **dean**.
sub: When the tongue is high and toward the back of the mouth and the lips are rounded, the result is the vowel in **dune**.
When the tongue is low, the result is an open vowel (a vowel with the mouth wide open), like the one in **Don**.
blocks.end: So the same sound from the vocal folds can become different vowels, because each constriction changes the formants.

blocks.main: **In the vocal tract, a constriction packs the air into a smaller space, so the air at that spot becomes both heavier (denser) and stiffer.** What the constriction does to a formant depends on what the air at that spot is doing in that mode (one particular pattern of vibration).
sub: To figure out the effect, first find where the constriction is. Then decide whether the air at that spot is mostly **moving** or mostly **compressed** in that mode.
If the air there is mostly moving, the extra mass is what matters. Heavier air is harder to move, so it vibrates more slowly, and the formant goes **down**.
If the air there is mostly compressed, the extra stiffness is what matters. Stiffer air springs back faster, so it vibrates more quickly, and the formant goes **up**.
blocks.end: So if a formant goes up a lot, the air at that spot was springy and hardly moving. If a formant goes down a lot, the air at that spot was moving a lot.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p19 · Lecture 13 · p16 · Lecture 14 · p11
blocks.main: **For /u/, as in dune, F1 and F2 both go down.** F1 is the first (lowest) formant and F2 is the second formant. **Lip rounding** makes a constriction at the lips, and the lips are the free end of the tube.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at the lips is moving, so the extra mass matters. Heavier air is harder to move, so **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at the lips is also moving, so the extra mass matters again. Heavier air is harder to move, so **F2 goes down**.
blocks.end: So at the lips only the extra mass matters, because the air at the lips moves in every mode.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p20 · Lecture 13 · p17, 21 · Lecture 14 · p12
blocks.main: **For /i/, as in dean, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** The constriction is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, which is near the front of the vocal tract.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot is moving, so the extra mass matters. Heavier air is harder to move, so **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is compressed, so the extra stiffness matters. Stiffer air springs back faster, so **F2 goes up**.
blocks.end: So the formants of /i/ **move apart**, because at that one spot, the air is moving in Mode 1 but compressed in Mode 2.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p21 · Lecture 13 · p18, 22 · Lecture 14 · p13
blocks.main: **For /a/, as in Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down.** The constriction is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, which is toward the back of the throat.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot is compressed, so the extra stiffness matters. Stiffer air springs back faster, so **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is moving, so the extra mass matters. Heavier air is harder to move, so **F2 goes down**.
blocks.end: So the formants of /a/ **move toward each other**, which is the opposite of what happens for /i/.

questions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I raise the formant a great deal, what must be true of air motion versus springiness at this location?
questions.a: If a constriction raises the formant a great deal, the air at that location must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode. This is because a constriction adds both mass and stiffness. The formant went up, so the added stiffness is what mattered. Stiffness only matters where the air is being compressed and expanded. The added mass did nothing, because the air there was not moving. So a big rise in the formant tells you the air at that spot was springy, not moving.

questions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I lower the formant a great deal, what must be true at this location?
questions.a: If a constriction lowers the formant a great deal, the air at that location must be moving a lot and hardly compressed in that mode. This is because the formant went down, so the added mass is what mattered. Mass only matters where the air is moving, because heavier air is harder to move and so it vibrates more slowly. This is what happens at the lips for /u/. So a big drop in the formant tells you the air at that spot was moving a lot.

questions.q: A classmate says more mass lowers the frequency and more stiffness raises it, so a constriction always cancels out. What is wrong with this argument?
questions.a: What is wrong with this argument is that, in any one mode, only one of the two changes matters at most locations. This is because the air at a spot is usually either mostly moving or mostly compressed. If the air at the constriction is mostly moving, it is not being compressed, so only the extra mass matters and the formant goes down. If the air there is mostly compressed, it is not moving, so only the extra stiffness matters and the formant goes up. So the two changes do not cancel out, and the same constriction can move F1 and F2 in opposite directions.

questions.q: Why is the air in the vocal tract a fixed-free system? Say which end is which.
questions.a: The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system because one end is closed and the other end is open. The glottis end is the fixed end, and the lip end is the free end. This is because the glottis end is closed off by the vocal folds. So the air there cannot move and can only be compressed and expanded. The lip end is open, so the air there moves freely in and out without being compressed against anything. So the closed glottis makes the fixed end and the open lips make the free end.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dune, and why?
questions.a: Compared with done, both F1 and F2 go down in dune. This is because lip rounding creates a constriction at the free end of the tube. At the free end, the air moves the most in every mode. So the added mass is what matters in both Mode 1 and Mode 2. Extra mass at a spot where the air is moving makes the air harder to move, so it vibrates more slowly. So both F1 and F2 have lower frequencies in dune.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dean, and why?
questions.a: Compared with done, F1 goes down and F2 goes up in dean. This is because the constriction is about two-thirds of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1, the air at that spot is moving, so the added mass makes it harder to move and lowers F1. In Mode 2, the air at that spot is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F2. So one constriction lowers F1 and raises F2, because the air at that spot does something different in each mode.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in Don, and why?
questions.a: Compared with done, F1 goes up and F2 goes down in Don. This is because the constriction is about one-third of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1, the air at that spot is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F1. In Mode 2, the air at that spot is moving, so the added mass makes it harder to move and lowers F2. So one constriction raises F1 and lowers F2, because the air at that spot does something different in each mode.

questions.q: A new constriction is placed deep in the throat, one-fifth of the way from the glottis, where the air is compressed in both Mode 1 and Mode 2. What happens to F1 and F2?
questions.a: If the new constriction is one-fifth of the way from the glottis, both F1 and F2 go up. This is because that location is near the fixed end. At that location, the air is compressed in both modes. So the added stiffness is what matters in both Mode 1 and Mode 2. Stiffer air springs back faster, so it vibrates more quickly. So both formants go up.

questions.q: Why does rounding the lips lower every formant?
questions.a: Rounding the lips lowers every formant because the lips are the free end of the vocal tract. This is because the free end is a location of maximum motion (where the air moves the most) in every mode. So a constriction at the lips adds mass where the air is moving. The heavier air is harder to move, so it vibrates more slowly, and that lowers every formant. Adding mass at the top of a building lowers every mode for the same reason. Since the air at the lips moves in every mode, every formant goes down.

topics.title: Spectra, spectrograms and speech over time

blocks.main: **A spectrum shows a sound at one instant, and a spectrogram lines up many spectra side by side over time.** In a spectrum, frequency is on the horizontal axis and amplitude (strength) is on the vertical axis. In a **spectrogram**, time is on the horizontal axis and frequency is on the vertical axis. The **darkness** of each spot shows the amplitude.
sub: The **dark bands on a spectrogram are the formants**, because the harmonics (the separate frequencies that make up the voice) near each formant are the loudest.
F1 is the lowest dark band, and F2 is the next dark band above it.
blocks.end: So the dark bands go up and down as the vocal tract changes shape.

blocks.main: **On a spectrogram, each vowel moves the formant bands in its own direction, starting from where they are for schwa.** Going from schwa to /i/, the bands **move apart**. Going from schwa to /u/, **both bands go down**. Going from schwa to /a/, the bands **move toward each other**.
sub: Going from /i/ to /a/, F1 goes up and F2 goes down.

blocks.main: **In connected speech (normal talking where sounds run into each other), the formants never stay still, because every sound changes the constriction.** In "Where were you a year ago?", F2 goes up when the tongue moves toward /i/. The formants go down when the lips round for the /u/ of you.
sub: When the tongue moves back and down toward an /a/-like sound, F1 goes up and F2 goes down.
blocks.end: So speech is a continuous series of constrictions, not a list of separate vowels.

blocks.main: **Listeners identify a consonant partly from the vowel that comes after it** (the vowel sound right after the consonant in the same syllable, not a vowel in the next word). In **Malécot**'s work in the 1950s, the m of ma was joined to the a of na. Listeners heard na.
sub: The a from na still contained the formant transition (the change in formant frequencies as the mouth moves from one sound to another) that was made by the n. Listeners used that formant transition to decide which consonant they heard.
blocks.end: So listeners decide which consonant they heard during the vowel, after the consonant is already over.

questions.q: Describe a spectrogram.
questions.a: A spectrogram is a display that lines up many spectra side by side over time. Time runs along the horizontal axis, and frequency runs up the vertical axis. The darkness of each spot shows how much amplitude (strength) there is at that frequency and that time. The formants (frequency regions with strong acoustic energy) appear as dark bands. So you can follow the formants as they go up and down, for example F1 going up and F2 going down from /i/ to /a/.

questions.q: How is a spectrum different from a spectrogram?
questions.a: A spectrum is different from a spectrogram because a spectrum shows one instant, while a spectrogram shows how the spectrum changes over time. A spectrum has frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. A spectrogram has time on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis, and it shows amplitude as darkness. Real speech is always changing. So a spectrogram lets you see the formants moving over time.

questions.q: A speaker starts on schwa and switches to another vowel. F1 goes down and F2 goes up. Which vowel? What if both go down?
questions.a:
When F1 goes down and F2 goes up, the vowel is /i/ as in dean. This is because the constriction for /i/ lowers F1 and raises F2, so the two bands move apart.

When both F1 and F2 go down, the vowel is /u/ as in dune. This is because lip rounding makes a constriction at the lips, where the air moves in every mode. So lip rounding lowers every formant.

questions.q: Describe the spectrogram of a speaker going from schwa to the vowel of Don.
questions.a: On the spectrogram of a speaker going from schwa to the vowel of Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down. So the two lowest dark bands move toward each other. This is because the constriction for Don is one-third of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1, the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F1. In Mode 2, the air there is moving, so the added mass makes it harder to move and lowers F2. So the F1 band rises and the F2 band falls until they are closer together.

questions.q: Why do listeners hear na when the m of ma is joined to the a of na?
questions.a: Listeners hear na when the m of ma is joined to the a of na because the information about the consonant is mostly in the vowel that follows it. This is because the consonant changes the formants at the start of the vowel. After n, one formant of the vowel goes down, and after m, that formant stays flat. The a from na still has the formant change that the n made. So listeners decide which consonant they heard during the vowel, after the consonant is over, and they hear n.

topics.title: The sigmoid and where the idea came from

blocks.main: **In a neural network, the sigmoid is a function that takes a neuron's inner product and gives back a number between 0 and 1.** The inner product is the neuron's inputs multiplied by their weights and added up. A large negative input gives about **0**, which means the neuron is off. A large positive input gives about **1**, which means the neuron is on. An input of exactly 0 gives **0.5**.
sub: The sigmoid curve is flat at both ends and steep in the middle. So the same change in the input makes the biggest difference to the output near the middle.
Very different things can be perceived as the same, such as a friend with or without a hat. This matches the flat parts of the sigmoid, where very different inputs give almost the same output.
Very similar things can be perceived as different, such as USC and UCLA. This matches the steep middle of the sigmoid, where very similar inputs can give very different outputs.

blocks.main: **In the code, nn.Sigmoid goes after each hidden layer.** Each hidden neuron first computes its inner product and then applies the sigmoid to it. The sigmoid's output is what gets sent to the next layer.
sub: The last layer has no sigmoid, because its outputs go to the loss, and the loss turns them into probabilities.
Each hidden sigmoid value is between 0 and 1, but the values do not have to add up to 1. So they are not a probability distribution (a set of probabilities that add up to 1).
blocks.end: So when a sigmoid changes a hidden value, every later layer changes too, because each layer uses the outputs of the layer before it.

blocks.main: **The sigmoid comes from a discovery about real neurons.** **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for showing that **neurons are nearly digital**, which means a neuron is either firing or not firing. The sigmoid behaves the same way, because its output is either nearly off or nearly on.
sub: Many basic ideas in AI, including neurons, inner products and near-digital firing, come from discoveries about real brains.

questions.q: Where does the idea of the sigmoid come from?
questions.a: The idea of the sigmoid comes from biology. This is because Lord Edgar Adrian discovered that real neurons are nearly digital, which means they are either firing or not firing. He won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for this. The sigmoid copies this by turning any inner product into a number between 0 and 1. So, like a real neuron, a sigmoid neuron is either nearly off or nearly on.

questions.q: A hidden neuron's inner product is minus 2. Is its sigmoid activation closer to 0 or 1, and what does that mean?
questions.a: If a hidden neuron's inner product is minus 2, its sigmoid activation is closer to 0 than to 1. This is because the inner product is negative, and the sigmoid gives a value below 0.5 for any negative input. For minus 2, the sigmoid gives about 0.12. A value close to 0 means the neuron is mostly off. So the neuron fires only rarely.

questions.q: If one input to that neuron goes up through a positive weight, what happens to its linear activation and its sigmoid activation?
questions.a: If one input goes up through a positive weight, both the linear activation and the sigmoid activation go up. This is because the input is multiplied by a positive weight, so a larger input makes a larger product. That makes the inner product (the linear activation) go up. For example, if the weight is +2 and the input goes from 1 to 3, the product goes from 2 to 6. The sigmoid always goes up when its input goes up. So the sigmoid activation goes up too, and the neuron fires more often.

questions.q: What is the sigmoid activation if the linear activation is exactly 0?
questions.a: If the linear activation is exactly 0, the sigmoid activation is 0.5. This is because the sigmoid curve is centered on an input of 0. Negative inputs give values below 0.5, and positive inputs give values above 0.5. So an input of exactly 0 lands in the middle, at 0.5. That value is halfway between 0 (off) and 1 (on), so the neuron is half active.

questions.q: How does the sigmoid match human perception?
questions.a: The sigmoid matches human perception because some very different things are perceived as the same, and some very similar things are perceived as different. This is because the sigmoid has flat parts and a steep middle. The flat parts give the same output for very different inputs, such as minus 100 and minus 1000. The steep middle gives very different outputs for two nearly equal inputs on either side of zero. So the flat parts match treating different things as the same, and the steep middle matches treating similar things as different.

blocks.main: **An LLM (large language model) is built from layers, and each layer contains heads.** A **layer** is one round of improving the vectors (the lists of numbers that represent the words). The layers come one after another from the input to the output. A **head** is one expert, and it is a set of weights. The heads sit side by side inside each layer.
sub: Each head gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors.
The layer combines the opinions of all its heads into improved vectors. Then the next layer does the same thing again with those improved vectors.

blocks.main: **Heads and layers work like visiting a series of classes to improve yourself.** The classes you visit one after another are the **layers**. The students in each class, who each give you an opinion, are the **heads**.
sub: Layers give an LLM **depth**, which means one round of improvement after another.
Heads give an LLM **width**, which means many experts are asked at the same time in each round.

blocks.main: **Predicting the next word is so hard that large systems have a hundred or more layers, with about a hundred heads in each layer.** Every one of those heads learns.
sub: If the predicted next word is wrong, every head in every layer adjusts its weights using backpropagation (the method that calculates how much each weight contributed to the error). This makes the next prediction closer to the right word.

questions.q: What are heads, and how do they relate to layers?
questions.a: A head is one expert, which is a set of weights that gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors. Heads sit side by side inside each layer. The layer combines all of its heads' opinions into improved vectors. The layers come one after another from the input to the output. So each layer uses its heads to improve the vectors again.

questions.q: In the classroom of experts, what are the classes and what are the students?
questions.a: In the classroom of experts, the classes are the layers and the students are the heads. This is because you visit the classes one after another, just as the layers come one after another. The students in each class each give a separate opinion at the same time, just as the heads in one layer work side by side. You combine those opinions before moving on to the next class. So each class is one layer, and each student in it is one head.

questions.q: Which gives an LLM depth and which gives it width, heads or layers?
questions.a: Layers give an LLM depth, and heads give it width. This is because layers are rounds of improvement that come one after another, which adds depth. Heads work side by side inside the same layer, which adds width. So more layers means more rounds, and more heads means more experts in each round.

questions.q: An LLM has 5 layers with 4 heads in each layer. How many heads does it have, and which of them work at the same time?
questions.a: The LLM has 20 heads, and the 4 heads inside the same layer work at the same time. This is because each of the 5 layers has 4 heads, and 5 times 4 is 20. The 4 heads inside one layer work side by side. The layers come one after another, so layer 2 works on the vectors that layer 1 improved. So heads in the same layer work at the same time, but heads in different layers do not.

questions.q: The LLM predicts bark instead of barks after "the dog that my parents ... ". Which weights change?
questions.a: When the LLM predicts bark instead of barks, the weights of every head in every layer change. This is because backpropagation calculates how much each weight contributed to the wrong prediction. Then each weight is adjusted a little in the direction that reduces the error. So the next prediction is closer to barks.

questions.q: Where is the knowledge of an LLM stored?
questions.a: The knowledge of an LLM is stored in its weights. This is because each head is a set of weights, and those weights are what change when the model learns. So the knowledge is spread across all the heads in all the layers. The vowel network's knowledge is stored in its weights in the same way.
